stories.primary_headline: IMA urges CBFC to deny certification to Sunny Deol-starrer, says film glorifies violence against medics

primary_source.headline: IMA urges CBFC to deny certification to Sunny Deol-starrer, says film glorifies violence against medics
primary_source.content:
New Delhi: The Indian Medical Association (IMA) has urged the Central Board of Film Certification (CBFC) to refuse certification to the upcoming Hindi film Suryaa: Ant Se Aarambh Tak, alleging that its teaser glorifies violence against doctors.In a representation to the CBFC chairperson dated November 4, IMA national president Dr Anilkumar J Nayak said the film, starring Sunny Deol and Ravi Kishan, attributes corruption to doctors as a class and presents assaulting doctors and hospital personnel inside a hospital as a "justified and heroic act."Directed by M Padmakumar, the film is scheduled for a nationwide theatrical release on November 20. Its official teaser was released on YouTube on October 19.The IMA said the teaser contains dialogues alleging that doctors charge exorbitant amounts, conduct unnecessary tests and accept commissions instead of writing prescriptions."Doctors don't write prescriptions; they write their commissions," the lead character says in the teaser, according to the representation.It also objects to scenes showing the lead character physically assaulting doctors, nursing staff and hospital personnel inside a hospital, claiming that such acts are presented as heroic and justified."The Film is likely to incite the commission of offences against doctors and other healthcare professionals, is against the interests of public order, involves defamation of registered medical practitioners as a body, and glorifies and justifies violence against doctors," the representation said.The association cited incidents of attacks on healthcare professionals across the country, including the stabbing death of a 22-year-old intern, Dr Vandana Das, in Kerala in May 2023, the assault on a doctor at a hospital in Kozhikode in October 2025 and attacks on resident doctors in Aligarh and Mumbai this year.'Satluj' director Honey Trehan criticises new CBFC guidelines, calls them 'cowardness and dictatorship'
It also cited a survey of 1,566 healthcare workers by experts from VMMC and Safdarjung Hospital and AIIMS, reported in May 2026, which found that 58.2 per cent of them felt unsafe at their workplace and 78.4 per cent had faced threats while on duty.The IMA said assaults on doctors by patients, relatives and attendants are a recurring feature of Indian hospitals and that the potential of the film to incite violence must be assessed in the prevailing conditions.It argued that violence in hospitals affects the community at large as attacks can disrupt medical services, endanger patients awaiting treatment and create an atmosphere of fear among healthcare workers.The association said the film violates Section 5B of the Cinematograph Act, 1952, which prohibits certification of films that are against public order, involve defamation, or are likely to incite the commission of an offence.It also cited the revised Guidelines for Certification of Films for Public Exhibition issued on September 16, arguing that the film violates provisions prohibiting glorification or justification of violence, depiction of visuals likely to incite offences and content involving defamation of an individual or a body of individuals.The IMA said the film's "objectionable" content forms its core theme and cannot be removed through mere excisions.It requested the CBFC to exhibit the film before IMA representatives and allow a medical expert nominated by the association to view it along with the examining committee.The association also sought an opportunity to be heard before any certification decision is taken and urged the board to refer the film to a revising committee if the examining committee recommends certification.The IMA said the film had not been submitted to the CBFC for certification as of October 22, according to the Information and Broadcasting Ministry.

brief_bullets: The Indian Medical Association has petitioned the Central Board of Film Certification to withhold clearance from the upcoming Hindi film Suryaa: Ant Se Aarambh Tak, starring Sunny Deol, arguing its teaser normalizes and glorifies violence against healthcare workers. Led by national president Dr Anilkumar J Nayak, the medical body asserts that the M Padmakumar-directed project defames practitioners as corrupt and depicts hospital assaults as heroic acts, violating Section 5B of the Cinematograph Act. Citing a pervasive climate of fear and recent high-profile attacks on medical professionals nationwide, the IMA warns that the theatrical release risks inciting real-world hostility and severely disrupting public order.
why_it_matters_bullets: The controversy highlights mounting tensions over media depictions of professional corruption and the precarious safety conditions of healthcare workers.

stories.primary_headline: Officials inspects cloud kitchens, hotels and sweet manufacturing units in Dakshina Kannada

primary_source.headline: Officials inspects cloud kitchens, hotels and sweet manufacturing units in Dakshina Kannada
primary_source.content: Mangaluru: Following instructions from Health and Family Welfare Minister U T Khader, a team led by Dakshina Kannada District Food Safety Designated Officer Dr Praveen Kumar CH, conducted inspections at the franchise units of shops that supply and sell cakes and ice creams sourced from cloud kitchens and central cake manufacturing units.The inspections were carried out in Surathkal jurisdiction. Officials collected cake samples for laboratory analysis to test whether colours are being used. Maharashtra FDA suspends 19 food licences; acts against Patanjali distributor over 'adulteration'Officials issued warnings against using harmful artificial colours to make cakes visually attractive. Manufacturers were asked to maintain quality and hygiene standards, without the addition of artificial colours while preparing sweets.During the drive, surprise raids were also conducted on local hotels to check kitchen cleanliness. Samples of raw materials and ingredients used in food preparation were sent to the laboratory for testing, and notices were served to establishments failing to maintain  hygiene.

stories.primary_headline: Airtel sees churn in customer base due to tariff change, plans more capex on data centre

primary_source.headline: Airtel sees churn in customer base due to tariff change, plans more capex on data centre
primary_source.content: New Delhi: Bharti Airtel has seen a "churn" in its customer base on a quarter-on-quarter basis, following its recent move to shift towards premium mobile plans, a senior company official said on Friday.Airtel has restored the Rs 299 entry-level plan with reduced data benefits after an increase in subscriber churn from its network.The app and website of Airtel have started displaying an option for the Rs 299 plan recharge that will remain valid for 28 days and offer 1 GB data per day instead of the 1.5 GB earlier."The churn that we are seeing in Q2 (second quarter) is for us – largely is combination of two things - the seasonality of Q2 that comes in as well as tariff interventions that we took, where there is always a temporary impact on customer continuity," Bharti Airtel, Managing Director and Chief Executive Officer, Shashwat Sharma said during company's earning call.According to analysts, Bharti Airtel net subscriber addition declined in the September quarter mainly on account of the company's strategy to move towards premium plans."Net subscriber adds, however, declined QoQ from 3.3 million to 0.7 million on account of higher churn (up from 2.6 per cent to 2.9 per cent), likely on account of the plan rationalisation step taken in August 2026, which involved discontinuation of the Rs 299 entry-level prepaid smartphone plan," Citi Research said in a report.Sharma said that usual tariff hikes have worked well for the company's quality customer base."I would say I don't see a constraint in terms of headroom or direct growth, etc that we have, and if ever this happens, we firmly believe we will continue to build industry-leading ARPU in this business," he said.Bharti Airtel's India mobile service revenue in the second quarter ended September 30, 2026, has increased by 10.1 per cent year-on-year, driven by customer additions on a year-on-year basis and average Revenue Per User (ARPU) expanding to Rs 271 in Q2 FY27 from Rs 256 in Q2 FY26, the company said.'Applied 5 years ago': Airtel ahead of Musk's Starlink in India's Satellite internet queue, says Sunil Bharti MittalAirtel's India customer base increased by about 11 per cent to 49.86 crore. The company's mobile customer base grew by 3.6 per cent to 37.72 crore, and home service, which includes fixed line broadband services, grew by about 29 per cent to 1.53 crore.Airtel's consolidated capex for the quarter stood at Rs 12,467 crore, including India capex of Rs 9,908 crore during the reported quarter.Bharti Airtel Executive Vice Chairman Gopal Vittal said the company's capital allocation on wireless networks has moderated."If you look at new towers being installed, it's very little now - less than a thousand in the ballpark of 500-600 sites this quarter. Of course, there will continue to be some expansion of 5G. Transport Capex tends to be large because a lot of fiberisation is being done within the company," he said.During the reported quarter, Airtel invested Rs 2,826 crore in a strategic land parcel for data centre expansion in India.Vittal said that the company will continue increasing capex in the data centre business and dividend payout."A lot of the incremental capex would really go behind the growth bets, which is data centres, as we spoke about and cloud. We have already announced a potential continued buyback in Airtel Africa. We've also done that in the Indus (Towers). So, that will continue. You will see that reflected in our conduct; dividend payouts will keep increasing over time," he said.Vital said that the land acquisition for data centres provides the company optionality over time of putting in at least a 400- to 500-megawatt plant."It's a large tract of land, and also it's concentrated in the right locations where the demand seems to be high. We will continue to look at other options for land and build out, as some of that demand from the US may get directed towards India," he said.Vittal said a lumpy capex would be earmarked over the next 12 to 18 months for data centre build-out in Visakhapatnam.

stories.primary_headline: Songs from the Firefront by Tim Winton review – climate urgency verges on panic, with moments of wonder too

primary_source.headline: Songs from the Firefront by Tim Winton review – climate urgency verges on panic, with moments of wonder too
primary_source.content: The masterful Australian writer has become a kind of prophet – and his dramatic and moving new essay collection challenges us not to look awayTim Winton has been working his themes for almost 50 years in a palimpsest of 32 books: family, manhood, land and ocean; what it is to be human and Australian; intimate pleasures and anxieties that feed his fiction. The distinctive quality of his new collection of memoir and essays, Songs from the Firefront, is urgency verging on panic. He’s an elder in his 60s, with limited time to get his messages across before we all go up in flames.Living on the western edge of Australia, Winton has been an eloquent climate-change activist for decades. He has fought, with tenuous success, to protect Ningaloo Reef. He entrances us with Scheherazade stories that blend crystalline nature writing and terrifying facts. The loss has accelerated now, he says, and the danger is immediate.Songs from the Firefront by Tim Winton is out now through Hamish Hamilton/Penguin Continue reading...

sources.headline: Songs from the Firefront by Tim Winton review – climate urgency verges on panic, with moments of wonder too

brief_bullets: Renowned Australian author Tim Winton has released a new essay and memoir collection, Songs from the Firefront, published by Hamish Hamilton and Penguin. Drawing on decades of environmental activism and a nearly fifty-year literary career, Winton blends crystalline nature writing with alarming ecological realities to warn of accelerating climate collapse. Living on Western Australia's coast, the sexagenarian writer uses his platform to challenge readers not to look away from immediate environmental threats, particularly the endangerment of the Ningaloo Reef. This urgent publication underscores the growing intersection of literature and climate advocacy as veteran cultural figures increasingly leverage their prestige to sound the alarm on ecological devastation.
why_it_matters_bullets: The book amplifies cultural urgency around climate change, mobilizing literary influence to drive ecological action.
